item.title: I Am Risen for the Shrimp
item.description: The State of Exception is over. The States of Exception have only begun.
item.content:encoded:
I know, I know — I haven’t been blogging for the better part of six months, and it’s been an unparalleled tragedy across these United States of Exception. I hear it’s even worse than all the fish reproduction in the Hudson River.

I may not be able to muster up an excuse, but I owe you all an explanation. I haven’t been blogging because I didn’t want to. On the occasion that something offended me on a visceral level, like Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu’s illegal war of aggression against Iran, I deigned to make a post about it.

Otherwise, I’ve been dedicating myself more or less full time to the very incremental task of nudging U.S. food, agricultural, and wildlife policy in a more humane direction, and doing the handful of things that are more efficient than keeping a Substack at raising my profile among the people who are influential enough to advance my career and help me accomplish more in the future. You might understand that writing an anonymous blog about heterodox foreign policy and dream welfare doesn’t dovetail too nicely with acquiring political influence.

Still, I had to return to Substack for this hallowed day. Last year, after ’s now (in)famous shrimp post helped raise nearly $20,000 for the Shrimp Welfare Project, I christened November 15th “International Shrimp Welfare Day.” Since then, , , and the rest of the crew at FarmKind have rebranded it “International Shrimpact Day” and extended it to a full week (November 25th through December 2nd), and recruited a slate of influencers to make it a truly worldwide phenomenon.

Participating bloggers are competing to raise money for the Shrimp Welfare Project. (For the likely minority of readers who aren’t aware, the Shrimp Welfare Project is a highly cost-effective charity that reduces the suffering of farmed shrimp who are raised at high concentrations in poor quality water and slaughtered while still conscious. It may sound weird, but the best evidence we have points toward shrimp feeling pain.) There’s an overall goal to raise $100,000, which is just over 3% of the organization’s 2024 revenue. There’s also a Substack Live debate tomorrow featuring Jeff Sebo, Lyman Stone, and Peter Singer (see here), and another on Sunday with Bentham’s Bulldog, Jeff Maurer, and Josh Szeps (see here).

If you’re already aware of the Shrimp Welfare Project and convinced to donate, please use my promo link to get a 50% match on your donation. The page also gives you a list of all participating bloggers (whose articles I’ll be linking to in another post at the end of the week), and more info about the charity.

As I promised when I announced the contest, I’ll be donating a total of $200 in the name of the blogger who raises the most money, who raises the most relative to their subscriber count, and who makes what I deem to be the most interesting argument for shrimp welfare. Hopefully those are all me, and I’m not above using underhanded tactics like emotional manipulation to make it happen. (By the way, if you don’t want to hurt my feelings after I ended my Substack hiatus just for you, you can go to this link to donate or press the shiny button below this paragraph to put “United States of Exception” at the top of The Shrimpact™ Leaderboard.)

You know you want to.

My official contest entry will (hopefully) come soon. Despite having a full year of advance notice, I still haven’t written it yet.

item.title: Spare the Shrimp, Spoil the Steer
item.description: RFK Jr. as a hero to shrimpkind.
item.content:encoded:
This article was written for International Shrimpact Day, a Substack-based fundraiser and competition organized by FarmKind to support the Shrimp Welfare Project. I’d appreciate it if you’d make a contribution and share this article as widely as possible. Every dollar donated to the Shrimp Welfare Project spares an estimated 1,400 shrimp per year from excruciating methods of slaughter.1 You can donate with a 50% match by following this link to the competition page, or by pressing the very alluring button below this paragraph.

Maximize Your Shrimpact

Sometime in December, the federal government is expected to release the 2025–2030 Dietary Guidelines for Americans, the government’s official advice to our fat stupid countrymen about what to shove down your disgusting gullet. The guidelines are ideally written according to the latest research in food and nutrition science, but almost always shaped by political pressure and industry lobbying. This year, they’re expected to be heavy on beef and whole milk — partly to own the namby-pamby liberals who care about ruminant methane emissions, partly because Donald Trump and Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins need to keep U.S. ranchers happy while they bail out the Argentine beef industry to prop up Argentina’s right-wing government, and partly because Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., and his gang of Victorian witch doctors think that the Standard American Diet doesn’t contain enough saturated fat. (They also think people should drink more, or at least don’t care about alcohol or sodium, don’t think people need more fiber, and don’t care about added sugar as long as it’s not corn syrup. They also might be bringing back the absurdly unscientific and fundamentally ill-designed food pyramid.)

Animal welfarists are understandably concerned about the new dietary guidelines. In April, Kennedy threw out a report by the Dietary Guidelines Advisory Committee that called for replacing animal-source proteins high in saturated fat with low-fat, fiber-rich proteins like beans, peas, and lentils. The Trump regime is also suffused throughout with meat and dairy industry interests that have spent much of the past year delivering on top animal agriculture and factory farm priorities, including faster line speeds at slaughterhouses, a rollback on food safety rules, approval for the Brazilian-owned meatpacker (and Trump donor) JBS to be listed on the New York Stock Exchange, bailouts for companies that exterminate millions of birds at risk of bird flu, support for overturning state animal welfare laws, extended subsidies for methane gas, and even more welfare payments for fish farms, fisheries, and Alaskan whalers in the Big Beautiful Bill. Nutrition expert and mother of food politics Marion Nestle interprets Rollins and Kennedy’s vow to exclude “leftist ideology” from the guidelines as a dog whistle to industry and conservative voters that they’re going to prioritize red meat and won’t be saying anything about plant-source foods.

Activists are right to be worried insofar as the new guidelines are poised to increase beef and dairy consumption and the number of cattle raised for food (as well as ruminant greenhouse gas emissions, which are plausibly very bad but probably not worse than factory farming). Still, we shouldn’t expect the new guidelines to be bad for animals overall. That’s because when people eat more red meat, they eat fewer smaller-bodied animals like chickens, fish, and — you guessed it — shrimp. In fact, because nearly every other animal product is more suffering-intense than beef and dairy, the more Rollins and Kennedy can do to promote the cattle industry, the more good they’ll do for farmed animals.

Maximize Your Shrimpact

Why does it matter? Many federal programs, including the National School Lunch and Breakfast Programs, WIC, and the military food services, use the dietary guidelines to determine what foods can be procured, served, and recommended using federal dollars. Direct federal food procurement alone is responsible for $9 billion in purchasing power per year, including more than $3.5 billion on animal products, $1 billion each on beef and poultry, and $500 million on fish and shellfish. Federal nutrition programs (including those above) account for another $140 billion for a total of 14% of U.S. grocery spending and nearly 6% of overall food expenditures.

The guidelines are also widely used by policymakers, medical professionals, and journalists to shape the cultural zeitgeist around food and nutrition. It’s obviously difficult to tease out causality between research, culture, and politics, but almost every major phenomenon in popular food and nutrition science over the past half century has either been set off, reflected, or reinforced by the dietary guidelines. In 2000, the government issued the first dietary guidelines recommending that Americans minimize trans fats in their diet. By 2008, there was an episode of King of the Hill about banning trans fats in Arlen. By 2013, the FDA initiated the process of banning trans fats nationwide, which it concluded by 2018.

Let’s say Rollins and Kennedy’s advice that Americans eat more beef and dairy can somehow restore U.S. per capita beef and milk consumption to record levels. Since the 1970s, per capita beef consumption has fallen by more than one-third, and fluid milk consumption has halved. The national cattle inventory is also at its lowest point in more than 50 years, or less than 100 million head (versus 2 billion chickens and 500 million farmed fish). Even if the dietary guidelines double per capita beef and dairy consumption, they’ll only result in another 100 million cattle being raised for food at any time.

If that was the whole story, that would be very bad! Dairy is very scary, beef is even scarier, and 100 million is a big number. But Americans don’t simply eat more beef and dairy without making any other changes to their diet. Since the 1970s, while beef consumption has fallen by a third, chicken consumption has almost doubled, seafood consumption has increased by half, and total meat consumption has remained the same since 2000. In kilogram terms, consumers make a nearly one-to-one substitution between beef and chicken, and a smaller substitution between beef and seafood.

If consumers actually heed the new guidelines and replace some share of their lean animal protein with beef and dairy, it would end up being very good for most farmed animals. According to the Faunalytics Animal Product Impact Scales, it takes about 0.58 chicken lives and 28 days of suffering to produce a kilogram of chicken meat. For fish, it’s 0.23 lives and 75 days of suffering. For shrimp, it’s 61 lives and 9,134 days of suffering (or more than 25 shrimp-years). For beef, it’s just 0.003 lives and 3 days of suffering.

For every 1% of lean animal protein replaced with beef, consumers could spare about 100 million chickens, 15 million fish, and 400 million shrimp from slaughter per year, as well as avert more than 60 billion suffering-days net of any additional days of cattle suffering. If you weight suffering-days for animal sentience according to the Rethink Priorities’ Welfare Range Estimates, then the suffering averted by lower chicken, fish, and shrimp consumption is still nearly 10 times as much as the suffering caused by increased cattle farming — and that’s an underestimate because the conditions of other farmed animals are much worse than the conditions of farmed cattle.

Does this make Kennedy and Rollins (the latter once dubbed a “psychopathic ghoul” and “evil hag” by Shrimpstack’s own Bentham’s Bulldog) heroes to shrimpkind? In a perverse way, yes. Anyone who saves 400 million shrimp must be a hero to the shrimp even if they’re a villain to cows, dogs (or goats), whales, Central Park bears, women, babies, and everybody else.

That’s a tough pill to swallow, but it’s also cause for action. If someone as repugnant as Kennedy can be a hero to the shrimp, then what’s stopping you? It only takes $1 donated to the Shrimp Welfare Project to help 1,400 shrimp per year (for up to 10 years) by providing electric stunners to producers to render shrimp unconscious before slaughter and getting retailers to source only stunned shrimp. That’s less than $150,000 to match the likely impact of the dietary guidelines over the five years they’ll be in place. If — and only if — you help raise $150,000 for the Shrimp Welfare Project, then you can confidently say you’re a better person than Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. If not, then we’ll all be left to wonder.

As of press time, International Shrimpact Day has raised around $20,000 for the Shrimp Welfare Project, not counting a generous 50% match. If you want to help us meet our goal and prove your moral bona fides, you can donate by following this link to the competition page, or by pressing the button below this paragraph.

Maximize Your Shrimpact

1

This is the median of a highly uncertain but conservative estimate. For more details and a full accounting, see here.

item.title: RFK Jr. Wants to Make You Eat Bugs
item.description: You can have my Red 40 when you pry it from my cold, red hands.
item.content:encoded:
For some reason, the Substack text to speech only reads the first 2:35 of the article. You can use the file above to listen to the whole thing.

I know what you’re thinking. Yeah, yeah — another Substacker coming at me with a clickbait title trying to get me to subscribe to his shitty newsletter.

Please subscribe to my shitty newsletter!

Didn’t you just tell me RFK Jr. is a hero to the shrimp? What’s this about bugs? And why don’t you ever write about the state of exception?

Allow me to explain myself in the form of a dirty limerick:

The man from Nantucket, a friend of the shrimp —
Who, when not spouting fiction, would find him quite limp —
For all his distraught
O’er the Davos bug plot,
Would still have us slurping on worms like his gimp.

What I’m trying to say here is that RFK Jr. wants to make you eat bugs. You might be skeptical given the disproportionate share of anti-bug-eating sentiment that comes from people like RFK Jr. who don’t even believe in the germ theory of disease. But trust me: This time, it’s real.

Due to a largely under-the-radar policy change initiated this spring, food manufacturers may soon be adding insect-derived dyes to countless products offered for sale in the United States. This could result in billions of insects being farmed for dye and trillions more being killed in the production process each year. Although research is scarce, there’s a good chance that some of these insects are capable of feeling pain. If so, the likely proliferation of insect-derived dyes may be the single most underrated calamity of the second Trump regime.

In this post, I try to share much more than you wanted to know about food dyes, estimate just how bad things might be, and engage in some very preliminary strategizing about how to mitigate harms to insects. I think this issue is very important, so please share it with anyone you know who might be in a position to do something about it. I especially recommend reading this post if you’re a funder or professional in food systems and you care about insect welfare. If you want to follow up privately on anything in this post, please DM me on Substack or contact statesofexception@proton.me.

Subscribe now

In September, the so-called “Make America Healthy Again Commission” chaired by RFK Jr. released a strategy report on children’s health. Among the more than 120 proposed reforms to U.S. food, agricultural, and health policy, it calls for the removal of artificial dyes from food products approved for sale by the FDA.

Here’s the MAHA Commission’s exact recommendation to President Trump:

In April, Kennedy and FDA Commissioner Marty Makary announced that the government would begin working with the food industry to eliminate artificial dyes by the end of 2026. Several large food manufacturers, including General Mills, Kraft Heinz, and Kellogg, have since pledged to remove artificial dyes by the end of 2027, the effective date of a MAHA-inspired law banning the dyes in West Virginia. California and Virginia have also enacted laws banning artificial dyes from school meals.

One of the dyes, Red 40, is primarily used in place of beet juice and carmine, an extract obtained by boiling or heating adult female cochineal insects alive and crushing their bodies for pigment. While beet juice is sometimes preferred because it costs less by volume, isn’t a known allergen, and fits halal, kosher, and vegan diets, carmine is often used because of its more vibrant and stable color and unnoticeable flavor.

Subscribe now

Okay, so what?

Abraham Rowe estimates that between 4 billion and 18 billion adult female cochineals are farmed for carmine each year. Additionally, between 4.6 trillion and 21 trillion nymphs and males are spawned and killed as part of the production process but not used for dye. Most of these are nymphs who die within 3 to 5 days after being spawned by farmed females. According to Rowe’s desk research, most of them likely die of starvation.

While no known research to date addresses the likelihood of cochineal sentience, there is evidence that adult and even juvenile members of some insect species fulfill several criteria associated with feeling pain, and no known evidence that any insects fail on any criterion. Even if there’s a 1% chance that cochineals feel pain, and they feel just 1% as much pain as other farmed animals, cochineal farming may cause as many as 6.3 billion to 10.5 billion sentience-adjusted suffering-days in expectation per year, or more than the entire global force-fed foie gras industry.1

While reliable market research is difficult to come by, experts widely believe that the dye phaseout is likely to result in carmine being added to more products. Many manufacturers that still use Red 40 prefer carmine to beet juice because it keeps its color in extreme temperatures and under extended light exposure and low pH. Some industry experts even refer to carmine as “the gold standard for natural reds.”

So how much more cochineal farming will we need to replace Red 40?

In the 19th century, before the development of artificial dyes, historians estimate that carmine exports from the Canary Islands alone reached as high as 3,000 metric tons per year. In 2018, the Embassy of Peru told BBC that the country exported 647 tons of carmine and controlled 95% of the international market. In fiscal year 2025, the FDA reported certifying nearly 8.4 million pounds of Red 40 in the U.S. food and drug supply, or 3,800 tons. A recent analysis found that 14% of all products marketed by the top 25 U.S. food and beverage manufacturers in 2020 contained Red 40, representing at least tens of billions of dollars in annual sales.

It’s widely reported that harvesting a pound of carmine requires killing 70,000 cochineals. However, this claim is poorly sourced and (according to Brian Tomasik) appears to come from a 1948 article about premodern cochineal production. It also excludes nymphs and males who are spawned and killed during the production process but not used directly for dye. Assuming that 700 metric tons of carmine are produced worldwide per year and between 15 and 25% of this is farmed rather than wild-harvested, Rowe’s estimates suggest that on the order of 10 million to 90 million cochineals are killed for a pound of carmine, and this includes between 10,000 and 70,000 adult females.

ChatGPT guesstimates that you need at least twice as much carmine by mass to get the same color intensity as Red 40. In 2013, researchers estimated the mass of artificial dyes in various sugar-sweetened beverages sold in the United States, with results of up to 52.3 mg of Red 40 per 8-ounce serving for the most dyed beverage, Kool-Aid Burst Cherry. If you replaced Red 40 with carmine, achieving the same color intensity would require putting the remains of between 2.3 and 16 cochineals in a drink and killing an additional 2,300 to 20,000 nymphs and males. Assuming again that there’s a 1% chance that cochineals feel pain, and they feel 1% as much pain as other farmed animals, that means a single serving of cherry Kool-Aid dyed with carmine would cause as many sentience-adjusted suffering-days in expectation as 0.2 to 3.3 kg of beef or 0.4 to 5.7 kg of pork, according to the Faunalytics Animal Product Impact Scales. Compare this to the Red 40 concentration of other drinks below.

Subscribe now

If the FDA certifies 3,800 tons of Red 40 in the U.S. food supply each year, and you need twice as much carmine to replace it, then for every 1% of FDA-certified Red 40 replaced with carmine, worldwide cochineal farming will have to increase on the order of 20 to 40%. That’s going to require killing billions of additional farmed cochineals and trillions of nymphs and males every year, and conservatively result in hundreds of millions or billions of sentience-adjusted suffering-days in expectation. (And just to put it in writing, that’s bad.)

So what is to be done?

One thing that’s not going to happen: RFK Jr., the FDA, and states that have enacted restrictions on artificial dyes aren’t going to reverse course. Nor are food and beverage manufacturers going to start making dye-free products just to sell in states with dye bans and keep them the same everywhere else. If just West Virginia stops permitting artificial dyes, it sets the standard for the whole country. Barring the unforeseeable, Red 40 going away ain’t going away.

There are two conceivable ways around the ban, and neither of them is likely to work.

First, artificial dye companies can challenge states’ dye restrictions in the courts. In October, the International Association of Color Manufacturers sued West Virginia officials in federal district court, claiming that the West Virginia dye ban usurps the FDA’s authority to regulate food safety and unconstitutionally infringes on interstate commerce. However, experts say the challenge is unlikely to succeed as the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act doesn’t expressly prohibit states from restricting food additives, and the West Virginia law doesn’t discriminate against out-of-state manufacturers.

Second, the food industry can lobby Congress to strip states of the right to regulate food additives and ingredient labeling. Some companies are already trying this through a coalition ironically called “Americans for Ingredient Transparency,” but so far nobody in Washington is willing to bite. Senator Roger Marshall, the founder and chair of the Congressional MAHA Caucus, planned to include federal preemption in a food additives bill he introduced in November, but removed the provision after facing unprecedented pushback from MAHA influencers and a wide range of consumer advocacy organizations.2 (Yes, that’s the Moms for Liberty one line under something called the “Society of Latinx Nurses.”) As Marshall told the New York Times last month: “I couldn’t believe how much pushback I got.”

Subscribe now

In fact, the only person in Washington who’s signaled openness to food additive preemption is RFK Jr., who recently told a reporter that a national food standard is “on the table for discussion.” This may be because, on the off chance that either industry lawsuits or lobbying efforts do succeed, they would only tee off another battle at the FDA that industry is likely to lose. MAHA is a must-win constituency for Republicans in 2026 and 2028, and restricting or banning artificial dyes is among the most popular items on the MAHA agenda, so Trump may just give RFK Jr. free reign over artificial dyes and sideline the corporate lobbyists.

To wit: In June, 80% of Americans said they support new restrictions on artificial dyes, with just 2% saying there should be no change to product formulation or packaging rules. In July and August, 85% of parents said they support “increasing government regulations on dyes and chemical additives in food.” As RFK Jr.’s former communications director and MAHA Action CEO Del Bigtree stated in a recent New Yorker profile of a MAHA influencer, “the food issue” has become such a critical part of the MAHA agenda because it’s popular enough to launder in more controversial policies like banning vaccines.

Subscribe now

Yes, but what should we do?

The best way to address the Red 40 ban almost certainly isn’t going to be saving Red 40 (which was already on the way out before legislation started to codify consumer sentiment), but disincentivizing and restricting carmine as manufacturers search for alternatives to artificial dyes. Much like the wider animal protection movement, this effort can be advanced by various public-facing, corporate, and governmental efforts, as well as support for alternative dyes that don’t involve farming insects.

First, activists can work to shift the narrative around carmine by linking it to widespread disgust at “eating bugs” and politically valanced alarmism over the Great Reset conspiracy theory. In practice, this could mirror recent narrative shifts around microplastics, ultra-processed foods, and other food dyes and additives including Red 40. These campaigns have all benefitted from slick public relations efforts that have amplified alarmist claims through earned and social media by leveraging sympathetic influencers, researchers, and policymakers. Many of the most prominent figures in the MAHA movement (the “MAHA Moms”) got their start spreading health misinformation online and branding hard-to-pronounce food additives as “toxic” or “poison” to drum up large audiences of concerned parents. The so-called “Food Babe,” Vani Hari — a key ally and informal advisor to RFK Jr. — broke into the mainstream in 2013 when she bit a yoga mat in a highly sexualized YouTube video to draw attention to the common bread additive azodicarbonamide, which is also used in yoga mats as a foaming agent. The following year, Subway announced that it was removing azodicarbonamide from its bread offerings.

Once artificial dyes are phased out, MAHA influencers will need a new bogeyman for their scientifically illiterate and dopamine-addled audiences. You can bet that they won’t be too thrilled to hear that Big Food is only taking out artificial dyes so they can make you eat bugs instead. Some deep-pocketed funder who cares about cochineals should consider dropping some five or six figures on a PR firm to recruit the MAHA Moms to sound the alarm about the little red bugs.

Second, activists should adopt the über-successful corporate campaign model used for caged eggs, crated pork, unhealthy chicken breeds, and ablated shrimp and deploy it against companies that dye foods with carmine. These campaigns might even present an opportunity to mainstream insect welfare — the ultimate radicalism — though they’d be more successful focusing on gross-out narratives about eating bugs. Regardless, all the technical details could be carried over from pre-existing campaigns. Activists behind the scenes could engage corporate leadership, draft policies, and propose shareholder resolutions to extract carmine-free commitments, and then escalate to public “naming and shaming” campaigns as necessary.

It wouldn’t even be the first time activists have targeted corporations for using carmine. In 2012, after a vegan recipe blog and associated Change.org petition blew the whistle on carmine use in Starbucks Frappuccinos, the chain announced that it was removing carmine from the menu a month later. In 2013, the Center for Science in the Public Interest ran a campaign against Dannon calling on the company to remove carmine from its yogurt. The campaign failed but did force Dannon to respond defending its use of insect-derived additives.

Third, activists can lobby Congress and the FDA to strengthen labeling requirements or revoke authorization for carmine as a food additive. In 2009, the FDA adopted a rule requiring food manufacturers to list either “carmine” or “cochineal” on ingredient labels instead of just “color added.” Since 1998, the Center for Science in the Public Interest has been pressuring the FDA either to ban carmine altogether or require “insect origin” labeling due to carmine’s incompatibility with halal, kosher, and vegan diets and moderate to severe allergen risk. Research suggests that between 0.7 and 3% of consumers and 40% of people with routine exposure exhibit allergic reactions to cochineal-derived dyes. This compares to just 0.2 to 2.9% of consumers with allergies to any one of the “Big 9” major allergens that federal law requires manufacturers to identify in bold print.

Subscribe now

Adding carmine to the major allergen list would require Congress passing legislation recognizing carmine alongside more conventional allergens like dairy, eggs, and nuts. This is unlikely, as the total number of carmine allergen incidents per year is significantly less than those of other major allergens, but still not impossible. In 2021, due to advocacy by Food Allergy Research & Education, Congress amended the law to require boldface labeling of sesame, which is only allergic to 0.2% of consumers. As long as major food allergy organizations are on board for labeling carmine, there’s a good chance that it could happen.

Counterintuitively, it may actually be easier for cochineal advocates to ban carmine altogether than require tougher labeling. Congress vests the FDA with unilateral authority to revoke authorization for food additives — effectively for any reason — under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. In January 2025, the agency revoked authorization for Red 3 due to evidence that it causes cancer in rats, even though the agency’s top food regulator admitted that the same effect “does not occur in humans.” In September, the agency initiated the revocation of Orange B due to the additive becoming obsolete. The FDA likewise could initiate the revocation of carmine due to allergy risks or alarmism over globalist conspiracies to make you eat bugs.

Finally, activists can support the development of insect-free (and preferably cheaper and allergen-friendly) natural alternatives by industry researchers. Food companies have increasingly looked toward plant-source and precision fermented natural dyes since the FDA started banning artificial dyes earlier this year. In an ideal world, there’d be enough money for a Good Food Institute for alternatives to insect-derived products. Barring that, some insect-concerned impact investors may be interested in promoting the alternative natural red dye industry.

In conclusion…

RFK Jr. wants to make you eat bugs. That’s very bad, and activists can respond by disincentivizing carmine use through cultural, corporate, governmental, and technological interventions. We just need to act quickly before companies reformulate their products and start using carmine more widely.

This ought to be a major priority among those who care about insects. Yet, no major figures or organizations in food systems or insect welfare appear to be working on this issue at all or even raising the alarm about RFK Jr. putting bugs in your food. In the eight months since the dye phaseout was announced, there have been zero posts (and just three comments) on the EA Forum including the words “carmine,” “cochineal,” or “Red 40.” To my knowledge, this is the first and only article about the welfare implications of the dye ban that’s been published anywhere this year. (And while that’s good and all, it shouldn’t be up to a lowly dirty limerick writer like me to be raising awareness.) While I suspect that a handful of organizations may be strategizing behind the scenes, that still leaves out most funders and professionals who could be taking coordinated action on this high-priority, time-sensitive issue while it still matters.

As the very failed Substacker Amos Wollen tells us, we’re living at the hinge of insect history. As things stand now, Red 40 is set to be eliminated by all of the largest U.S. food and beverage manufacturers by January 1, 2028. It can either be replaced by other synthetic or plant-source dyes, or it can be replaced by carmine. If you give any non-negligible credence to the experience and wrongness of cochineal suffering, then you should care immensely that we go down the right path.

Subscribe now

Share

1

In 2012, the Humane Society of the United States (now Humane World for Animals) estimated that 700,000 geese and 37 million ducks are slaughtered each year for foie gras. These animals are typically slaughtered at 14 weeks, implying roughly 3.7 billion suffering-days per year.

2

Animal welfarists should also steer clear of supporting federal preemption to avoid alienating these potential partners or giving any ammunition to supporters of the so-called “Food Security and Farm Protection Act” and “Save Our Bacon Act,” which would overturn dozens of state animal welfare laws and force millions of chickens and pigs back into tiny cages.

item.title: America Still Goes to War for Self-Esteem

Well, here we go again. By my count, this is at least the sixth time that Trump has crept up to the precipice of war with Iran. Every other time, he’s had some sniveling pinko commie whispering into his ear to let him know that when you creep up to a precipice, you’re not actually supposed to jump in. For a while, this woke make-work job was cut by DOGE and rolled into the portfolio of secretary-cum-advisor-cum-administrator-cum-archivist-cum-sock-cum-rag Marco Rubio. They only brought the pinko back last summer when they realized he’s the only one who knows the number to the closest pizza place to the Pentagon. They also figured out that you can drown out almost anything with the bombastic adenoidal screeching of that fat, balding sack of shit Mark Levin.

Yes, America has gone to war with Iran, and it’s about damn time. We’ve been due for some excitement going on 20 years now, only our stupid and pathetic leaders have been too stupid and pathetic to understand that you can just do things. The late so-called “President” Joe Brandon (or whoever ran the autopen) suffered a particularly extreme strain of the neurosis that afflicted his boss, the Kenyan Muslim Communist Barry Soetoro Obummer. “Uhhh, let me be queer, Jack. I’m a weak liberal and I hate Israel and America. I wear a tan suit and I’ve been to 57 states. I ruined the military by transing all the soldiers and making them gay-marry Mexicans. I’m gay and my wife is a man.”

Are you triggered yet? Cry more, lib. Your reign of gayness is over. Don’t you know we got 200,000 votes in the same three goddamn states in the Upper Midwest? I’m nothing if not a hipster, so as I understand the kids are saying these days: “Let’s go suck and fuck Joe Brandon.” America is back, baby. Mothers, lock up your daughters, or at least don’t send them to school. Good job Pete and your team!!

You might be asking why Iran and why now. The short answer is fuck you, that’s why. The long answer is that Uncle Sam is a declining power in the grips of a crippling self-esteem crisis and he needs an outlet to prove that he’s still the toughest guy on the block, and Iran is simply the most convenient target. If it wasn’t Iran, it would be Cuba or Mexico or Greenland — any crappy little country would suffice. Yes, the liberal international order is dead, and yes, long live the liberal international order!

Does it have to be any more complicated than that? America is mired in an era of bad feelings. We’ve seen this one before, and it ends the same every time. I won’t say I saw this one coming, but I offered a fairly prescient observation over a year ago when I said that America goes to war for its self-esteem:

After Vietnam, America was stuck in some deep psychological doo-doo. Norman Podhoretz — a neoconservative intellectual whom the libertarian economist Murray Rothbard once compared to a Joseph Heller character “whose sole literary output is a series of autobiographies celebrating his own life and thought” — complained that the Vietnam Syndrome had rendered even the likes of Henry Kissinger and Gerald Ford into isolationist surrender monkeys. Reagan and Bush tried to pull America out of its funk by bombing a hospital in Grenada and blasting Guns N’ Roses at the CIA’s old friend Manuel Noriega’s hideout in Panama, but it took a right proper war with right proper social mobilization — slick Kuwaiti propaganda, round-the-clock TV coverage, Whitney Houston belting the national anthem, etc. — to do the trick.1 According to political scientist John Mueller, the broad-based destruction of the bombing in Iraq, compounded by sanctions after the war, killed more people than chemical, biological, and atomic weapons had killed in all of human history. (And Poppy’s approval rating climbed to 89%.)

So, too, was America in some doo-doo after 9/11.2 This was temporarily resolved by the second Iraq War, which served the enemies of freedom worldwide, from Phil Donahue to the Dixie Chicks, their due comeuppance.3 “The Right Brothers,” a pro-war conservative rock duo from Nashville, won acclaim for their 2005 single, “Bush Was Right.” It declared, not in so many words, that the Ledeen Doctrine had succeeded —

Democracy is on the way, hitting like a tidal wave
All over the Middle East, dictators walk with shaky knees
Don’t know what they’re gonna do
Their worst nightmare is coming true
They fear the domino effect, they’re all wondering who’s next

— and yes, that America was back. Meanwhile, the opposition leader on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, a 60-year-old whippersnapper by the name of Joe Biden, told the Brookings Institution that his harshest criticism of the administration was that the president hadn’t leveled with the American people and told them: “We have to finish the job.”

Maybe you know how the rest of the story goes. At some point, America got a loser stink. Obummer and Brandon pulled out when they should have fucked them all to death. Don’t you get it? It’s the Bigger Dick Foreign Policy Theory. “What, they have bigger dicks? Bomb them!”

Again, I don’t mean to say I told you so, but I don’t know how else to put it. More from me a week after the inauguration:

America’s ongoing crisis of confidence is among the most dangerous trends in the world today. It wasn’t enough to push Biden into a Ledeenian-style war for self-esteem, but that’s just because he had some practicality left in his rapidly diminishing mind. Not so for his successor. Foreign policy experts fear that when Xi Jinping speaks of Chinese “national rejuvenation,” it’s a euphemism for international belligerence and territorial expansion. They should be at least as concerned when Trump talks about an American “Golden Age.” In his inaugural address, he threatened to steal the Panama Canal and expand American territory, “to once again act with courage, vigor, and the vitality of history’s greatest civilization.” He constantly talks about annexing Canada and invading Greenland as projects of national renewal. During his first week in office, he threatened tariffs and sanctions against Canada, Mexico, Denmark, Russia, China, Colombia, and the European Union.

Then there are his advisors: Pete Hegseth likens himself to a crusader. Mike Waltz — once an advisor to Dick Cheney — advocated a 100-year war in Afghanistan framed as a civilizational battle between good and evil. When Marco Rubio, America’s new top diplomat, ran for president in 2016, he lifted his campaign slogan, “A New American Century,” from the name of the neoconservative think tank, the Project for the New American Century, that served as a government-in-waiting for the George W. Bush administration and drafted the blueprints for the Iraq War.4 At his confirmation hearing, Rubio asserted that the “post-war global order” — supposedly defined by the usurpation of American national interests to a rootless cosmopolitanism — is not only “obsolete,” but a “weapon” being employed against the United States by bad actors like China and Iran.

Let us grant this conspiracy of knaves and dunces an undeserved benefit of the doubt: say they don’t want a war. How else is this supposed to end? Since 1945, the peace has been kept by American economic and military preponderance — ironically sustained by the United States restraining itself to avoid provoking allies and adversaries into militarization — unprecedented commercial globalization, norms of territorial integrity, and mutually assured destruction. The Trump regime promises to undermine every one of these pillars. You cannot remain preponderant by estranging your allies while antagonizing your enemies. You cannot maintain globalization by further weaponizing the international trade and financial system. You cannot uphold international norms by trampling them with impunity. You cannot preserve the balance of terror and pursue nationwide missile defense at the same time. Something has to give: either the Long Peace or the Long March for American Greatness.

A deceptive alternative is to attempt to remain aloof of great power conflict and instead pursue a “splendid little war” in the Western hemisphere or a good, hard thrashing of the Iranians in retaliation for their never having thanked us for getting half a million of them killed in the 1980s. If not Panama or Greenland, Rubio surely has a list of targets he’d like to strike in Cuba, Venezuela, and any other paisito de mierda under a leftist administration. Waltz wants to go for Mexico. Trump says: “Stranger things have happened.” The Wall Street Journal reports the president is “weighing options” to bomb Iran. During his first administration, he toyed with the idea as late as two weeks before leaving office.

But a feel-good strike against a crappy little country is also a strike against the pillars of international peace. There aren’t enough carrots and sticks in the world to make it go down easy with allies or adversaries. Maybe you could buy off some votes in the U.N. General Assembly, but that’s about it. The Chinese get the moral high ground, and with our resources tied up in the desert or the Caribbean, it becomes a lot harder to stop them from taking Taiwan.5 Meanwhile, the Russkies, having just gone through their own Afghanistan in Ukraine (not to be confused with their other own Afghanistan) might see fit to put us on the receiving end of a proxy war for once — and at some point, the sky’s the limit on the escalation ladder.

It feels anachronistic to be talking about a great power war, but that’s where we’re at. The American people got in a funk, and they chose the Insane Clown Posse to cheer themselves up. This isn’t like the first Trump administration, which kept some semi-competent experts around who slow-walked or shot down the president’s worst ideas, and didn’t have four years ahead of time to cook up a revisionist fever dream. This isn’t even like the Bush administration, which wanted to rough up some international miscreants but didn’t know they’d have the opportunity until it arrived. No, this is America’s Golden Age.

For the time being, however, we’re still a nation of bad vibes. Someone needs to reckon with it, and bad cess to them. Crappy little countries round the world, beware: it seems that you’re overdue for a thrashing.

Well, maybe I got ahead of myself at the end there, although I am speaking probabilistically, and there’s plenty that I got right and plenty more that could prove right in due time. Soon enough we’ll get tired of winning and find out. Until then, have a happy war, and thank you for your attention to this matter — we sure showed those libs what’s what.

A particularly amusing anecdote from philosopher Paul Patton’s introduction to Jean Baudrillard’s volume The Gulf War Did Not Take Place:

At the time, the TV Gulf War must have seemed to many viewers a perfect Baudrillardian simulacrum, a hyperreal scenario in which events lose their identity and signifiers fade into one another. […] Occasionally, the absurdity of the media’s self representation as purveyor of reality and immediacy broke through, in moments such as those when the CNN cameras crossed live to a group of reporters assembled somewhere in the Gulf, only to have them confess that they were also sitting around watching CNN in order to find out what was happening. Television news coverage appeared to have finally caught up with the logic of simulation.

It seems worth noting that the 9/11 attacks possibly never would have occurred if the United States hadn’t gone to war with Saddam in 1990–91, or if it had conducted itself more prudently in the war’s aftermath. Osama bin Laden’s 1996 and 1998 fatwas mentioned three overriding motivations for attacking the United States: that the United States maintained military bases in Saudi Arabia to enforce its Iraqi no-fly-zones; that it starved Iraqi children through its sanctions against Saddam; and that it supported Israel. These complaints were also the basis of most of al-Qaeda’s Arabic-language propaganda, meaning that even if they were a cynical fig leaf for bin Laden’s simply Hating Our Freedoms, they were apparently the genuine motivation of the bulk of his supporters. As political scientist Robert Pape found in his groundbreaking study of the motivations of suicide terrorism:

Most suicide terrorism is undertaken as a strategic effort directed toward achieving particular political goals; it is not simply the product of irrational individuals or an expression of fanatical hatreds. The main purpose of suicide terrorism is to use the threat of punishment to coerce a target government to change policy, especially to cause democratic states to withdraw forces from territory terrorists view as their homeland.

Donahue’s talk show was cancelled by MSNBC on February 25, 2003, supposedly due to low ratings. However, Donahue’s ratings were the highest of any program on the network. A leaked NBC internal memo stated that Donahue would be a “difficult public face for NBC in a time of war […] He seems to delight in presenting guests who are anti-war, anti-Bush and skeptical of the administration’s motives,” and expressed fear that Donahue’s show would become “a home for the liberal anti-war agenda at the same time that our competitors are waving the flag at every opportunity.”

Donahue was replaced by pro-war conservative shock jock Michael Savage, whose show was described by MSNBC president Erik Sorenson as “destination television for those looking for compelling opinion and analysis with an edge.” By July 2003, Savage was fired for saying to an on-air caller: “Oh, you’re one of the sodomites. You should only get AIDS and die, you pig. How’s that? Why don’t you see if you can sue me, you pig. You got nothing better than to put me down, you piece of garbage. You have got nothing to do today, go eat a sausage and choke on it. Get trichinosis.”

Although I am loath to cite the bumbling Thomas Friedman, the following quote from a recent column is instructive:

Question: “What does Xi Jinping feel when Trump starts talking about taking Greenland and the Panama Canal?”

Answer: “Hungry” — for Taiwan.
